title: Management Accounting
source_note: Grounded in standard management accounting curriculum: cost-volume-profit analysis, budgeting, standard costing and variance analysis, marginal vs absorption costing, relevant costing for short-term decisions, capital budgeting/investment appraisal, and performance measurement, as taught in NUC-aligned accounting programmes. Kept distinct from ACC203 (Cost Accounting I, which covers basic cost elements/costing methods) by focusing on internal decision-making and control uses of accounting information.

questions.question: How does management accounting primarily differ from financial accounting?
options: Management accounting provides information primarily for internal decision-making, planning, and control, and is not bound by statutory reporting formats
Management accounting is legally required to follow IFRS while financial accounting is not
Management accounting reports are always audited while financial accounting reports never are
Management accounting only deals with historical data while financial accounting only deals with forecasts
questions.correct_answer: Management accounting provides information primarily for internal decision-making, planning, and control, and is not bound by statutory reporting formats
questions.explanation: Management accounting serves internal users (management) for planning and control and can be tailored freely, whereas financial accounting follows statutory/regulatory formats for external users.
questions.topic: Nature and scope of management accounting

questions.question: What is 'contribution' in cost-volume-profit (CVP) analysis?
options: Sales revenue minus total variable costs
Sales revenue minus total fixed costs
Sales revenue minus total costs (variable and fixed combined)
Total fixed costs minus total variable costs
questions.correct_answer: Sales revenue minus total variable costs
questions.explanation: Contribution is the amount remaining from sales after deducting variable costs, which first goes towards covering fixed costs and then towards profit.

questions.question: At the break-even point, what is true of total contribution?
options: Total contribution exactly equals total fixed costs, so profit is zero
Total contribution equals total variable costs
Total contribution is always negative
Total contribution equals total sales revenue
questions.correct_answer: Total contribution exactly equals total fixed costs, so profit is zero
questions.explanation: By definition, break-even is the point where contribution generated is just enough to cover fixed costs, leaving neither profit nor loss.

questions.question: A product sells for ₦500 per unit, with variable cost of ₦300 per unit, and total fixed costs of ₦400,000. What is the break-even point in units?
options: 2,000 units
800 units
1,333 units
4,000 units
questions.correct_answer: 2,000 units
questions.explanation: Contribution per unit = 500 − 300 = ₦200. Break-even units = Fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit = 400,000 ÷ 200 = 2,000 units.

questions.question: What does 'margin of safety' measure?
options: The excess of actual or budgeted sales over the break-even sales level
The excess of fixed costs over variable costs
The difference between selling price and total cost per unit
The minimum profit a company is legally required to make
questions.correct_answer: The excess of actual or budgeted sales over the break-even sales level
questions.explanation: Margin of safety indicates how far sales can fall before the business reaches break-even and starts making a loss, expressed in units, value, or as a percentage of sales.

questions.question: Under 'marginal costing', how are fixed production overheads treated?
options: They are treated as period costs and written off in full against the profit of the period in which they are incurred
They are absorbed into the cost of each unit produced and carried forward in closing inventory valuation
They are ignored entirely and never appear in the financial statements
They are capitalised as a non-current asset
questions.correct_answer: They are treated as period costs and written off in full against the profit of the period in which they are incurred
questions.explanation: Marginal costing charges only variable production costs to units of output; fixed overheads are treated as period costs charged in full to the income statement.

questions.question: Under 'absorption costing', how are fixed production overheads treated?
options: They are absorbed into the cost of production and included in the valuation of inventory, so some fixed overhead can be carried forward to the next period
They are written off completely against profit in the period incurred, regardless of production levels
They are excluded from product cost and treated purely as a selling expense
They are only recognised when the related goods are exported
questions.correct_answer: They are absorbed into the cost of production and included in the valuation of inventory, so some fixed overhead can be carried forward to the next period
questions.explanation: Absorption costing shares fixed production overhead across units produced, meaning unsold units in closing inventory carry a portion of fixed overhead forward into the next period.

questions.question: If production exceeds sales in a period (inventory increases), how will reported profit under absorption costing compare with profit under marginal costing?
options: Absorption costing profit will be higher, because some fixed overhead is deferred in closing inventory rather than charged to the period
Absorption costing profit will be lower, because more fixed overhead is expensed
The two methods will always report identical profit regardless of inventory movement
Marginal costing profit will always be higher than absorption costing profit, regardless of inventory movement
questions.correct_answer: Absorption costing profit will be higher, because some fixed overhead is deferred in closing inventory rather than charged to the period
questions.explanation: When inventory rises, absorption costing carries forward a share of fixed overhead in the closing stock value, reducing the fixed overhead charged to the current period and thus reporting a higher profit than marginal costing.

questions.question: What is a 'budget' in management accounting?
options: A quantified plan of action for a defined future period, prepared and approved in advance
A historical record of actual costs incurred in the previous financial year
A statutory financial statement filed with the tax authority
An informal estimate that management is not expected to monitor
questions.correct_answer: A quantified plan of action for a defined future period, prepared and approved in advance
questions.explanation: A budget translates organisational objectives into a formal, quantified financial and/or operational plan for a future period.

questions.question: In the typical order of preparing a master budget, which functional budget is normally prepared first, since most other budgets depend on it?
options: The sales budget
The cash budget
The capital expenditure budget
The master budget itself
questions.correct_answer: The sales budget
questions.explanation: Because production, purchasing, labour, and most other functional budgets are driven by expected sales volume, the sales budget is normally the starting point of the budgeting process.

questions.question: What is a 'flexible budget'?
options: A budget that is adjusted to reflect the actual level of activity achieved, to allow a fair comparison with actual results
A budget that never changes once it has been approved
A budget prepared only for the sales department
A budget that ignores the effect of changes in activity level entirely
questions.correct_answer: A budget that is adjusted to reflect the actual level of activity achieved, to allow a fair comparison with actual results
questions.explanation: A flexible budget recalculates budgeted costs and revenues at the actual activity level, so variances reflect genuine efficiency or cost differences rather than just volume differences.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a 'cash budget'?
options: To forecast the timing and amount of cash inflows and outflows, helping management plan for cash shortages or surpluses
To record the actual cash transactions that occurred in the prior accounting period
To calculate the company's total assets at the year end
To determine the company's corporate tax liability
questions.correct_answer: To forecast the timing and amount of cash inflows and outflows, helping management plan for cash shortages or surpluses
questions.explanation: The cash budget is a planning tool that projects cash movements over a period so management can anticipate financing needs or surplus cash for investment.

questions.question: What is 'zero-based budgeting' (ZBB)?
options: A budgeting approach where every item of expenditure must be justified afresh for each new budget period, starting from a base of zero, rather than simply adjusting the prior year's figures
A budgeting approach where the budget is always set at zero for all departments
A method used only for capital expenditure budgets, never for operating budgets
A budgeting approach that ignores past performance entirely and uses random figures
questions.correct_answer: A budgeting approach where every item of expenditure must be justified afresh for each new budget period, starting from a base of zero, rather than simply adjusting the prior year's figures
questions.explanation: Unlike incremental budgeting, ZBB requires managers to justify all proposed spending each period, which can reveal unnecessary costs but is more time-consuming.

questions.question: What is 'standard costing'?
options: A costing technique that sets predetermined (standard) costs for materials, labour, and overheads, against which actual costs are later compared to calculate variances
A method of costing used only in service industries
A technique that records only actual historical costs, with no predetermined targets
A method that eliminates the need for a budgeting process
questions.correct_answer: A costing technique that sets predetermined (standard) costs for materials, labour, and overheads, against which actual costs are later compared to calculate variances
questions.explanation: Standard costing establishes cost benchmarks in advance for control purposes, enabling variance analysis by comparing actual results against these standards.

questions.question: The direct material price variance measures which of the following?
options: The difference between the standard price and the actual price paid per unit of material, multiplied by the actual quantity purchased
The difference between standard and actual quantity of material used, multiplied by the standard price
The difference between budgeted and actual sales revenue
The difference between standard and actual labour hours worked
questions.correct_answer: The difference between the standard price and the actual price paid per unit of material, multiplied by the actual quantity purchased
questions.explanation: The material price variance isolates the effect of paying more or less than the standard price per unit for the actual quantity of material bought.

questions.question: The direct material usage variance measures which of the following?
options: The difference between the standard quantity of material allowed for actual output and the actual quantity used, valued at the standard price
The difference between actual price paid and standard price, valued at standard quantity
The difference between budgeted output and actual output in units
The difference between fixed overhead absorbed and fixed overhead incurred
questions.correct_answer: The difference between the standard quantity of material allowed for actual output and the actual quantity used, valued at the standard price
questions.explanation: The usage variance isolates the effect of using more or less material than the standard allowance for the actual level of output achieved, holding price constant at standard.

questions.question: The direct labour rate variance measures which of the following?
options: The difference between the standard wage rate and the actual wage rate paid, multiplied by the actual hours worked
The difference between standard hours allowed and actual hours worked, multiplied by the standard rate
The difference between budgeted and actual production overhead
The difference between standard and actual selling price per unit
questions.correct_answer: The difference between the standard wage rate and the actual wage rate paid, multiplied by the actual hours worked
questions.explanation: The labour rate variance isolates the cost effect of paying a different hourly wage rate than standard, for the actual hours actually worked.

questions.question: The direct labour efficiency variance measures which of the following?
options: The difference between the standard hours allowed for actual output and the actual hours worked, valued at the standard rate
The difference between actual wage rate and standard wage rate, multiplied by standard hours
The variance arising solely from changes in raw material prices
The difference between actual and budgeted fixed costs
questions.correct_answer: The difference between the standard hours allowed for actual output and the actual hours worked, valued at the standard rate
questions.explanation: The labour efficiency variance measures whether the workforce took more or less time than standard to produce the actual output, valued at the standard labour rate.

questions.question: An adverse (unfavourable) material usage variance most likely indicates which of the following?
options: More material was used per unit of output than the standard allowed, perhaps due to wastage or lower-quality material
Material was purchased at a price below standard
Output was exactly equal to the budgeted level
Labour was more efficient than standard
questions.correct_answer: More material was used per unit of output than the standard allowed, perhaps due to wastage or lower-quality material
questions.explanation: An adverse usage variance means actual material consumption exceeded the standard allowance for the output achieved, commonly caused by wastage, spoilage, or inferior material quality.

questions.question: What is 'relevant cost' in short-term decision making?
options: A future, incremental cash flow that will change as a direct result of the decision being made
Any historical cost already incurred, regardless of the decision made
A cost that will be incurred whether or not the decision is taken
An allocated share of general fixed overhead that will not change with the decision
questions.correct_answer: A future, incremental cash flow that will change as a direct result of the decision being made
questions.explanation: Relevant costs are future, differential cash flows directly affected by a decision; sunk costs and unavoidable costs common to all alternatives are irrelevant.

questions.question: What is a 'sunk cost' and why is it excluded from relevant costing decisions?
options: A cost already incurred in the past that cannot be recovered or changed by any future decision, so it has no bearing on the current choice
A future cost that will definitely be incurred regardless of the decision, but is still relevant
A cost that varies directly with production volume
The opportunity cost of choosing one alternative over another
questions.correct_answer: A cost already incurred in the past that cannot be recovered or changed by any future decision, so it has no bearing on the current choice
questions.explanation: Because sunk costs cannot be altered by any future action, they are irrelevant to forward-looking decisions and should be ignored in relevant costing analysis.

questions.question: In a 'make-or-buy' decision, what is the correct comparison to determine whether a company should continue making a component in-house?
options: Compare the relevant (avoidable) cost of making the component internally with the price of buying it externally, considering only costs that would actually change
Compare only the direct material cost of making the item with the full purchase price
Always choose to buy externally if the supplier's price is lower than total absorbed cost, without adjustment
Always choose to make internally regardless of cost, to protect jobs
questions.correct_answer: Compare the relevant (avoidable) cost of making the component internally with the price of buying it externally, considering only costs that would actually change
questions.explanation: A sound make-or-buy decision focuses on relevant, avoidable costs of internal production versus the external purchase price, excluding unavoidable fixed overheads that would be incurred either way.

questions.question: When a single scarce (limiting) resource constrains production of multiple products, how should a company decide the optimal production mix to maximise profit?
options: Rank and prioritise products by their contribution per unit of the scarce resource, producing the highest-ranked products first
Rank products only by total contribution per unit sold, ignoring the scarce resource entirely
Produce equal quantities of every product regardless of profitability
Always prioritise the product with the highest selling price per unit
questions.correct_answer: Rank and prioritise products by their contribution per unit of the scarce resource, producing the highest-ranked products first
questions.explanation: When a resource such as machine hours or material is limited, profit is maximised by allocating that scarce resource to the products yielding the highest contribution per unit of the constraint.

questions.question: In a special/one-off order decision, when should a company accept an order priced below its normal full cost per unit (assuming spare capacity exists)?
options: When the price offered still exceeds the relevant (incremental) cost of fulfilling the order, and it does not adversely affect normal sales or capacity
Never, because price must always cover full absorbed cost
Only if the order matches or exceeds the normal selling price
Only if the customer is a related party
questions.correct_answer: When the price offered still exceeds the relevant (incremental) cost of fulfilling the order, and it does not adversely affect normal sales or capacity
questions.explanation: With spare capacity and no effect on existing sales, any price above the incremental relevant cost adds to overall contribution and profit, even if it is below normal full cost.

questions.question: What is 'responsibility accounting'?
options: A system that assigns revenues, costs, and performance to specific managers or responsibility centres who can be held accountable for controllable results
A system used only for preparing statutory financial statements
A method of allocating shared fixed overheads equally across all departments regardless of usage
An accounting method exclusive to non-profit organisations
questions.correct_answer: A system that assigns revenues, costs, and performance to specific managers or responsibility centres who can be held accountable for controllable results
questions.explanation: Responsibility accounting links financial results to the managers responsible for them, distinguishing between cost centres, profit centres, and investment centres.

questions.question: What distinguishes a 'profit centre' from a 'cost centre' in responsibility accounting?
options: A profit centre manager is responsible for both revenues and costs, while a cost centre manager is responsible only for costs
A profit centre manager is responsible only for costs, while a cost centre manager is responsible for both revenue and costs
A cost centre always generates more profit than a profit centre
There is no practical difference between the two terms
questions.correct_answer: A profit centre manager is responsible for both revenues and costs, while a cost centre manager is responsible only for costs
questions.explanation: A profit centre's performance is judged on the net profit it generates (revenue minus cost), whereas a cost centre manager is evaluated purely on cost control since they do not control revenue generation.

questions.question: What is 'transfer pricing' in management accounting?
options: The price charged for goods or services transferred between divisions or segments of the same organisation
The price a company charges an external, unrelated customer
The price at which shares are transferred between shareholders
A price set exclusively by external market regulators
questions.correct_answer: The price charged for goods or services transferred between divisions or segments of the same organisation
questions.explanation: Transfer pricing concerns internal pricing between divisions of the same entity, used to evaluate divisional performance and encourage goal congruence.

questions.question: In investment appraisal, what does the 'payback period' method measure?
options: The length of time required for the cumulative cash inflows from a project to equal the initial capital invested
The total profit a project will generate over its entire life
The rate of return that equates the present value of inflows to the initial investment
The accounting profit as a percentage of the average investment
questions.correct_answer: The length of time required for the cumulative cash inflows from a project to equal the initial capital invested
questions.explanation: Payback period is a simple measure of how quickly the initial outlay is recovered from a project's net cash inflows, ignoring the time value of money and cash flows beyond payback.

questions.question: What is the main criticism of the payback period as an investment appraisal technique?
options: It ignores the time value of money and disregards any cash flows occurring after the payback point
It is too complex mathematically for most managers to understand
It always favours long-term projects over short-term ones
It cannot be calculated without a computer
questions.correct_answer: It ignores the time value of money and disregards any cash flows occurring after the payback point
questions.explanation: Payback's simplicity is also its weakness: it does not discount cash flows and completely ignores profitability generated after the payback period.

questions.question: What does 'Net Present Value' (NPV) represent in capital investment appraisal?
options: The sum of the present values of all a project's future net cash flows, discounted at the company's required rate of return, minus the initial investment
The total, undiscounted cash inflow expected from a project over its life
The accounting profit reported in the year the investment is made
The market value of the assets purchased under the project
questions.correct_answer: The sum of the present values of all a project's future net cash flows, discounted at the company's required rate of return, minus the initial investment
questions.explanation: NPV discounts all expected future cash flows back to present value using an appropriate discount rate and compares this to the initial outlay to assess value creation.

questions.question: Under the NPV decision rule, when should a single, independent project be accepted?
options: When its NPV is positive (greater than zero)
When its NPV is negative
Only when its NPV is exactly equal to zero
Regardless of the sign of its NPV, as long as payback is quick
questions.correct_answer: When its NPV is positive (greater than zero)
questions.explanation: A positive NPV indicates the project's discounted cash inflows exceed its initial cost, meaning it is expected to add value for shareholders and should be accepted.

questions.question: What is the 'Internal Rate of Return' (IRR) of a project?
options: The discount rate at which the project's net present value equals exactly zero
The company's cost of capital, fixed regardless of the project
The accounting rate of return based on average annual profit
The rate of inflation expected over the life of the project
questions.correct_answer: The discount rate at which the project's net present value equals exactly zero
questions.explanation: IRR is the break-even discount rate for a project; if it exceeds the company's required rate of return (cost of capital), the project is generally considered acceptable.

questions.question: What does the 'Accounting Rate of Return' (ARR) method measure?
options: The average annual accounting profit generated by a project expressed as a percentage of the initial or average investment
The discounted cash flow return of a project over its entire life
The number of years it takes to recover the initial investment in cash terms
The market interest rate available on comparable investments
questions.correct_answer: The average annual accounting profit generated by a project expressed as a percentage of the initial or average investment
questions.explanation: ARR is based on accounting profit rather than cash flow and does not consider the time value of money, unlike NPV and IRR.

questions.question: What is 'Activity-Based Costing' (ABC) primarily designed to improve?
options: The accuracy of overhead cost allocation to products, by tracing overheads to the specific activities and cost drivers that cause them
The speed of preparing external financial statements
The calculation of a company's corporate tax liability
The process of raising external equity finance
questions.correct_answer: The accuracy of overhead cost allocation to products, by tracing overheads to the specific activities and cost drivers that cause them
questions.explanation: ABC assigns overhead costs to products based on the activities that actually drive those costs (cost drivers), giving more accurate product costs than a single volume-based overhead rate, especially where overheads are high and products are diverse.

questions.question: What is a 'cost driver' in Activity-Based Costing?
options: A factor that causes a change in the cost of an activity, used as the basis for allocating that activity's costs to products
The total budgeted cost of the finance department
A synonym for direct material cost
The person responsible for approving the annual budget
questions.correct_answer: A factor that causes a change in the cost of an activity, used as the basis for allocating that activity's costs to products
questions.explanation: A cost driver, such as number of machine set-ups or purchase orders, is the causal factor used to allocate an activity's pooled overhead cost to the products that consume that activity.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes 'semi-variable' (mixed) costs?
options: Costs that contain both a fixed element and a variable element that changes with activity level, such as a telephone bill with a fixed line rental plus a per-minute call charge
Costs that remain completely constant regardless of activity level
Costs that vary in exact direct proportion to output with no fixed component at all
Costs that only occur once, at the start of a business
questions.correct_answer: Costs that contain both a fixed element and a variable element that changes with activity level, such as a telephone bill with a fixed line rental plus a per-minute call charge
questions.explanation: Semi-variable costs combine a fixed base charge with a variable component that increases with usage or output, unlike pure fixed or pure variable costs.

questions.question: The 'high-low method' is used in management accounting primarily to do what?
options: Separate a semi-variable (mixed) cost into its fixed and variable components using the highest and lowest activity levels observed
Calculate the exact break-even point in units
Determine the optimal selling price for a new product
Calculate depreciation on non-current assets
questions.correct_answer: Separate a semi-variable (mixed) cost into its fixed and variable components using the highest and lowest activity levels observed
questions.explanation: The high-low method estimates the variable cost per unit from the difference in total cost between the highest and lowest activity periods, then derives the fixed cost element.
